title: How do you calculate weighted averages quickly in a case interview?
description: Weighted averages explained with case examples: blended margins, average prices across segments, and how mix changes move the average.
hook: Weighted averages appear in many cases, often without being named: a blended margin across products, an average price across customer groups. Getting them wrong is one of the most common maths slips. Here is how to get them right quickly.
body:
The idea

An ordinary average treats every item equally. A weighted average gives each item a weight, usually its share of sales or volume.

A worked example: blended margin

A company sells two products. Product A: £60M of sales at a 10% margin. Product B: £40M at a 30% margin.

Wrong: (10% + 30%) ÷ 2 = 20%. Right: (60 × 10% + 40 × 30%) ÷ 100 = (6 + 12) ÷ 100 = 18%.

Mix changes

Next year sales shift to £80M of A and £20M of B, with the same margins. Blended margin: (8 + 6) ÷ 100 = 14%. Profit falls from £18M to £14M even though total sales are flat and neither product's margin changed. This is a mix effect, and it is often the hidden answer to a profitability case.

A quick method

  1. Multiply each value by its weight.
  2. Add them up.
  3. Divide by the total weight.

Practise

Try: 70% of customers pay £10 and 30% pay £20. Average price? (0.7 × 10 + 0.3 × 20 = 7 + 6 = £13.) More in the practice questions.
